meta.label: Soccer (Football)
meta.indoorOutdoor: outdoor (grass or artificial turf); futsal/indoor variants exist
meta.contactLevel: moderate (tackling, shielding, aerial duels; contact managed by rules, not armoured)
meta.competitionFrequencyPerWeek: 1 match/week typical (amateur/club); 2 matches/week in congested professional periods (league + cup/continental)
meta.notes: Two 45-minute halves of near-continuous intermittent running: ~10-13 km per match with an activity change every 4-6 seconds and a sprint roughly every 90 seconds. The gym's job is availability and explosiveness — hamstring, groin and knee protection plus acceleration force — never to add conditioning the pitch already supplies. Hamstring strain is THE soccer injury; the Nordic + Copenhagen pillars are the best-evidenced prevention in any sport.

aerobicEndurance.why: ~10-13 km per match at a mean intensity near 85% HRmax (~70% VO2max); the aerobic engine drives repeat-effort recovery and protects late-match technical quality.

repeatSprintAbility.why: 150-250 brief intense actions per match with incomplete recovery; the decisive moments cluster — pressing sequences, transitions, defending counters.
repeatSprintAbility.source: Mohr 2003 (match activities of top-class players); Stølen 2005

acceleration.why: Most match sprints are <20 m from varied starts; straight sprinting is the single most frequent action preceding goals — for scorer and assister alike.
acceleration.source: Faude 2012 (straight sprinting most frequent action in goal situations); Haugen 2014

sprintSpeed.why: Breakaways, recovery runs and tracking wingers expose players to near-maximal velocity — the same exposure that injures unprepared hamstrings, so it must be trained, not avoided.
sprintSpeed.source: Haugen 2014 (sprint profiles of elite footballers); Malone 2017 (sprint exposure as protection)

deceleration.why: Pressing, closing down and re-cutting demand repeated maximal braking; eccentric capacity is the tissue armour for knee and hamstring.

changeOfDirection.why: ~700 turns and swerves per match; 1v1 elimination and defensive re-orientation pivot on sharp COD — also the dominant non-contact ACL mechanism.

explosivePower.why: Shooting, jumping for headers, 1v1 first steps and GK dives all express rapid force; squat strength and jump height correlate strongly with sprint performance in elite players.
explosivePower.source: Wisløff 2004 (strong correlation of maximal squat strength with sprint and jump in elite soccer)

anaerobicEndurance.why: Blood lactate of 2-10 mM in match play; glycolytic tolerance shapes the quality of repeated pressing bursts and late-half surges.

relativeStrength.why: Strength-to-bodyweight drives acceleration, braking and duel stability without carrying non-functional mass around 10+ km of running.

maxStrength.why: The foundation under power, braking and tissue robustness; soccer is not strength-limited, but stronger players sprint faster and jump higher at every level studied.

reactiveStrength.why: Stiffness for cutting and re-acceleration, jump-land quality in aerial duels; a targeted dose also underpins ACL-protective landing mechanics.
reactiveStrength.source: expert consensus (S&C panel); ACL neuromuscular-training literature

stability.why: Every kick is struck from single-leg stance; knee-over-toe control in plant-and-cut is the core of neuromuscular ACL prevention.
stability.source: FIFA 11+ component evidence (Bizzini & Dvorak 2015); Webster & Hewett 2018

balance.why: Soccer is a one-legged sport in disguise — striking, shielding under contact and landing all live on a single-leg base; balance training reduces recurrent ankle sprain.

mobility.why: Hip flexion/extension range for kicking amplitude and full sprint mechanics; hip-flexor and hamstring extensibility keep the striking action out of the lumbar spine and proximal tendons.

rotationalPower.why: The kick is a proximal-to-distal whip — pelvis and trunk rotation over a braced stance leg deliver ball speed; crossing and long passing scale with it.

coordination.why: Ball manipulation at speed under fatigue is the sport; gym work must arrive fresh enough never to blunt touch and striking quality.

neckStrength.why: Repeated heading and aerial-duel exposure; neck strength plausibly attenuates head accelerations, but protective evidence is emerging rather than established.

gripStrength.why: Minimal for outfield play (shirt-grappling aside); goalkeepers need catching/parrying hand strength, trained through GK-specific work.

energySystems.workToRestRatio: intermittent ~1:5 to 1:8 for high-intensity efforts embedded in near-continuous sub-maximal activity; an activity change every 4-6 s
energySystems.matchDemands: ~10-13 km total (position-dependent); high-speed running ~600-1200 m; sprint distance ~200-400 m with a sprint roughly every 90 s; 150-250 brief intense actions; ~700 turns; 30-50 kicks/duels
energySystems.heartRateProfile: Mean ~85% HRmax (range 80-90%); repeated periods >95% HRmax during pressing sequences and transitions; blood lactate 2-10 mM
energySystems.fatigueProfile: High-intensity running falls ~25-45% in the final 15 minutes of elite matches, with temporary dips after the most intense 5-minute periods; sprint quality, deceleration mechanics and technical actions degrade with it — the injury window opens late
energySystems.notes: Elite figures; amateur volumes are lower but the intermittent pattern is identical. The pitch supplies almost all conditioning — the gym's contribution is force, robustness and the qualities the pitch cannot safely dose (eccentric hamstring strength, adductor strength, maximal force).

movementProfile.jointLoading: High eccentric hamstring load at terminal swing in sprinting; high knee valgus/rotation exposure in plant-and-cut; adductor load in kicking follow-through and lateral pushing; repetitive ankle inversion exposure in tackles and landings
movementProfile.groundContacts: Very many sub-maximal contacts across ~10-13 km; regular maximal-velocity exposure (unlike smaller-pitch codes) — hamstrings must be prepared for it
movementProfile.landingDemands: Moderate — aerial duels and headers land on one leg in traffic; GK landing demand is high (dives, parries, crosses)
movementProfile.throwing: Throw-ins only (long-throw specialists aside); not a programming priority
movementProfile.jumping: Moderate-high — contested headers for all outfield roles, dominant for centre-backs and strikers; maximal and reactive for goalkeepers
movementProfile.cutting: Constant — 1v1 elimination, pressing angles, defensive re-orientation; the dominant non-contact ACL mechanism
movementProfile.rotating: Every strike of the ball rotates pelvis-to-trunk over a planted stance leg; shooting and crossing are rotational power expressions
movementProfile.overheadActions: Rare (GK excepted); overhead gym volume is postural balance, not sport transfer
movementProfile.collisions: Moderate — tackles, shoulder-to-shoulder duels, GK collisions in the box; managed by rules, not equipment
movementProfile.repeatedImpacts: Repetitive footstrike across long match distances; cumulative calf/Achilles and bone load, higher on artificial turf
movementProfile.asymmetricLoading: Kicking-leg dominance is near-universal: the striking leg accumulates hip-flexor/quadriceps load while the STANCE leg absorbs braking, rotation and adductor load — both sides carry sport-specific risk and both need auditing
commonDeficiencies: eccentric hamstring strength vs sprint exposure (the headline modifiable risk)
adductor strength vs kicking + cutting volume
single-leg knee control in plant-and-cut (valgus collapse)
hip-flexor/rectus femoris capacity vs kicking volume
calf capacity vs match running load

common.name: Hamstring strain
common.incidence: very high — THE soccer injury: ~12% of ALL time-loss injuries and ~37% of muscle injuries at professional level, and it has been RISING year-on-year
common.mechanism: high-speed running — eccentric overload of the terminal-swing phase; secondarily long kicking actions under stretch
common.rtpConsiderations: Criteria-based: restore eccentric strength symmetry, then progressive sprint reloading to >95% max velocity BEFORE match return; unreloaded returns drive the recurrence statistics.
common.source: Ekstrand 2011 (UEFA muscle-injury surveillance); Ekstrand 2016 (annual rise); Petersen 2011 + van der Horst 2015 (Nordic RCTs)

common.name: Adductor/groin strain
common.incidence: high — ~23% of muscle injuries at professional level
common.severity: moderate, recurrence-prone; can chronify into long-standing groin pain
common.mechanism: kicking follow-through under stretch, lateral pushing/cutting, and contested reach tackles
common.rtpConsiderations: Copenhagen-based strength restoration with squeeze-test tracking; rebuild kicking volume gradually — long/place kicking last.

common.name: ACL rupture
common.incidence: lower frequency but the highest-burden injury; ~2-3x relative risk in the women's game
common.severity: severe — season-ending (6-12 months), career-threatening recurrence risk
common.mechanism: ~70% non-contact: plant-and-cut or single-leg landing with knee valgus collapse and internal rotation, often when perturbed or fatigued
common.rtpConsiderations: Criteria-based, time-respecting (≥9 months materially lowers re-injury): strength symmetry, hop battery, on-pitch COD progression, psychological readiness.
common.source: Webster & Hewett 2018 (prevention meta-analysis); FIFA 11+ evidence (Bizzini & Dvorak 2015; Thorborg 2017)

common.name: Ankle sprain (lateral)
common.incidence: high — the most common joint injury
common.severity: low-moderate, strongly recurrence-prone (chronic instability if under-rehabbed)
common.mechanism: inversion under contact (tackles, landing on an opponent's foot) and unanticipated cuts

modifiable: incomplete rehab of a prior sprain

common.rtpConsiderations: Graded COD re-exposure + balance retraining; bracing/taping on return is evidence-supported and cheap insurance.

common.name: Quadriceps/rectus femoris strain
common.incidence: moderate-high — ~19% of muscle injuries; biased to the kicking leg
common.severity: moderate; proximal rectus femoris injuries can be slow (4-8 weeks)
common.mechanism: explosive kicking — the hip-extended, knee-flexed backswing loads rectus femoris under stretch; sprinting accelerations contribute
common.rtpConsiderations: Rebuild kicking volume like sprint volume — graded, counted, with long/place kicks reintroduced last.
common.source: Ekstrand 2011 (muscle-injury surveillance); expert consensus on kicking-load management

common.name: Calf/soleus strain and Achilles overload
common.incidence: moderate (~13% of muscle injuries), rising sharply with age and fixture congestion
common.mechanism: accumulated match running load, repeated push-offs; congested schedules without calf capacity
common.rtpConsiderations: Isometric → heavy-slow-resistance calf progression; graded return to full match distance.

injuryProfile.summary: Muscle strains dominate: hamstring (37%), adductor (23%), quadriceps (19%) and calf (13%) account for ~92% of all muscle injuries in the UEFA surveillance. The gym owns the two best-evidenced preventions in sport — Nordic (~50% hamstring reduction) and Copenhagen (~41% groin reduction) — plus neuromuscular ACL prevention. Availability is the transfer: the strongest predictor of team success in surveillance data is low injury burden.

positions.name: Goalkeeper
positions.role: Shot-stopping, commanding the box on crosses, 1v1 denial, distribution (now a passing position too).
positions.movementDemands: Explosive lateral dives, maximal vertical jumps, rapid get-ups, short bursts off the line; hundreds of low-intensity positioning adjustments.
positions.runningDemands: Lowest of any position (~4-6 km, almost all walking/jogging).
positions.collisionDemands: Highest single-event contact risk: crowded-box collisions, striker challenges, ground impacts from diving.
positions.powerReq: very high (dive push-off, vertical jump, get-up speed)
positions.strengthReq: moderate-high (impact tolerance, aerial duels under contact)
positions.bodyComposition: Tall and powerful; lean enough for repeated floor work and quick get-ups.
positions.recoveryConsiderations: Low running load — tolerates more gym volume than outfield players; manage hip/groin soreness from repeated diving.

positions.name: Centre-back
positions.role: Aerial dominance in both boxes, front-foot defending, duel winning, build-up passing.
positions.movementDemands: Repeated maximal jumps under contact, hard short accelerations to step in, emergency recovery sprints, physical duels.
positions.runningDemands: Lowest outfield total distance (~9-10 km) but high-consequence maximal sprints when exposed.
positions.collisionDemands: Highest outfield duel/contact volume — aerial challenges, shoulder duels, blocks.
positions.speedReq: moderate-high (rare but decisive recovery sprints at full velocity)
positions.powerReq: very high (aerial power decides both boxes)
positions.strengthReq: high (duel stability, shielding, holding off forwards)
positions.bodyComposition: Tallest, most powerful outfield build; mass must not cost recovery-sprint speed.
gymPriorities: eccentric hamstring (their sprints are rare, maximal, and unprepared — the classic CB injury)
positions.recoveryConsiderations: Duel bruising and jump-landing load; their sparse sprint exposure means DELIBERATE weekly high-speed running top-ups are protective, not optional.

positions.name: Full-back / Wing-back
positions.role: The corridor engine: overlap and underlap runs in attack, recovery sprints in defence, crossing supply.
positions.movementDemands: The highest repeat-sprint load in the team — continuous up-and-back corridor running, high-speed overlaps, maximal recovery sprints, crossing under fatigue.
positions.runningDemands: Highest high-speed-running and sprint distance of any position (~10-12 km total, sprint volume peaks here).
positions.speedReq: very high (top-end velocity is the job description)
commonInjuries: hamstring (the highest sprint exposure in the squad)
gymPriorities: eccentric hamstring capacity (Nordic) — non-negotiable at this sprint volume
minimal-dose strength that never blunts running quality
positions.recoveryConsiderations: Highest weekly sprint load in the squad — heavy posterior-chain gym work needs 48 h separation from sprint-dense sessions and matches.

positions.name: Central midfielder
positions.role: The link: circulation, pressing triggers, box-to-box support, second balls, tempo control.
positions.movementDemands: Near-continuous shuttling with constant turns (~700/match concentrate here), tight-space COD, press-and-recover cycles.
positions.runningDemands: Highest total distance (~11-13 km elite); moderate sprint distance but the most direction changes.
positions.recoveryConsiderations: Highest total running load — the gym must flex around pitch volume; prioritise quality micro-doses over added volume in-season.

positions.name: Striker / Forward
positions.role: Penetrating runs in behind, first-step separation, finishing, aerial threat, first line of the press.
positions.movementDemands: Explosive short accelerations from standing/curved starts, sharp COD to create shooting angles, maximal sprints in behind, repeated jumps in the box, high kicking (shooting) volume.
positions.runningDemands: Moderate total (~10-11 km) but the highest density of maximal accelerations and penalty-box explosive actions.
positions.collisionDemands: High — back-to-goal shielding against centre-backs, aerial duels.
positions.powerReq: very high (first step, shot power, aerial)
positions.bodyComposition: Fast-powerful; profile varies from target (mass) to runner (pace) archetypes.
gymPriorities: acceleration strength (hip thrust, sled, split squat)
positions.recoveryConsiderations: Shooting practice is quadriceps/adductor load — count it like sprint volume; separate heavy lifting from finishing-session days.

assessments.name: Countermovement jump (CMJ)
assessments.purpose: Lower-body power benchmark + weekly neuromuscular-fatigue monitor (drop vs rolling baseline) — doubly useful in congested fixture periods.
assessments.source: Claudino 2017 (CMJ for fatigue monitoring); Stølen 2005 (elite values)

assessments.name: 10 m / 30 m sprint
assessments.purpose: Acceleration (10 m) is the game's decisive action; 30 m captures near-maximal velocity, the hamstring-relevant exposure.

assessments.name: Yo-Yo Intermittent Recovery Test Level 1
assessments.purpose: THE soccer-specific fitness test: intermittent high-intensity capacity with active recovery, validated against match high-intensity running.

assessments.name: Repeated-sprint ability (6×35 m, 10 s turnaround)
assessments.purpose: Sprint decrement under incomplete recovery — the pressing/transition quality.

assessments.name: Nordic hamstring strength
assessments.purpose: Eccentric hamstring strength — the headline modifiable factor for soccer's number-one injury.
assessments.frequency: each block + after any hamstring flag

targets.elite: ≥400 N or full-control Nordic (male); symmetrical (<10% imbalance)

assessments.name: Adductor squeeze (45°)
assessments.purpose: Groin capacity benchmark + weekly early-warning monitor for the kicking/cutting load.

assessments.name: 505 change-of-direction test
assessments.purpose: Deceleration + turn quality — the COD half of soccer speed, and a useful post-ACL benchmark.

assessments.name: Back squat / trap-bar deadlift (3-5RM est.)
assessments.purpose: Global strength anchor — maximal squat strength correlates strongly with sprint and jump performance in elite players.

assessments.name: Single-leg calf raise capacity
assessments.purpose: Calf strength-endurance vs match running load; the veteran-injury (soleus/Achilles) screen.

highest: bodyweight strength (lunge, hinge, push, pull, land)
landing/cutting quality (the ACL window is adolescence — especially girls)
youth.trainingEmphasis: Athletic literacy first; FIFA 11+ Kids-style neuromuscular warm-ups are proven, free and habit-forming. Growth-spurt years need patience with COD load.
commonMistakes: conditioning children instead of building strength foundations
unmanaged kicking-volume spikes in shooting-heavy sessions
skipping landing mechanics with adolescent girls — the highest-return ACL window

highest: eccentric hamstring habit (Nordic) BEFORE senior sprint volumes arrive
development.trainingEmphasis: Build the tissue the senior game will tax: hamstrings, adductors, calves, single-leg control. The prevention pillars become permanent habits here.
commonMistakes: skills-only development with no strength base
introducing senior sprint loads without eccentric hamstring preparation

highest: availability (the best ability): Nordic + Copenhagen + calf pillars every week
strength maintenance at minimal effective dose
senior.trainingEmphasis: Protect the match: gym work flexes around pitch load and fixture congestion, never compounds it.
commonMistakes: stacking gym volume in congested weeks
dropping prevention pillars when fixtures compress (exactly when risk peaks)
no deliberate high-speed-running top-ups for low-exposure players (centre-backs, GKs)

highest: squad-level rotation + load planning across competitions
elite.trainingEmphasis: Individualised, monitored, minimal-dose development around a 50+ match calendar; the physical programme is availability management.
commonMistakes: letting cup congestion erase prevention pillars
returning hamstrings to matches without maximal-velocity reloading

highest: calf/Achilles + tendon care (the veteran injury profile)
masters.trainingEmphasis: Retain power and tissue capacity; respect the slower recovery curve; keep playing.
commonMistakes: sprinting cold in the first minutes of veterans' matches
ignoring calf capacity — the age-defining tissue

offSeason.primaryObjective: Rebuild max strength, hamstring/adductor/calf capacity and aerobic base; fix the season's asymmetries and niggles.
offSeason.trainingEmphasis: Max strength + targeted hypertrophy; eccentric robustness work at full dose (the soreness window nobody minds); aerobic base cross-training.

programming.source: soccer S&C: off-season rounds out (upper balance) + max-strength base; in-season prehab-heavy (Nordic/Copenhagen van Dyk 2019), congested-fixture aware

preSeason.primaryObjective: Convert strength to acceleration/power; rebuild high-speed-running tolerance progressively (the hamstring-protective exposure); reach match fitness without the classic pre-season injury spike.
preSeason.trainingEmphasis: Power + speed conversion; progressive sprint exposure to >95% max velocity; Nordic/Copenhagen doses established before friendly congestion.
preSeason.recoveryEmphasis: moderate-high (pitch load rising fast — the riskiest ACWR window of the year)

programming.source: soccer S&C: off-season rounds out (upper balance) + max-strength base; in-season prehab-heavy (Nordic/Copenhagen van Dyk 2019), congested-fixture aware

competition.primaryObjective: Maintain qualities at minimal effective volume; maximise match availability across ~40 weeks.
competition.trainingEmphasis: 1-2 short heavy-but-low-volume sessions anchored to match day (MD-4/MD-3); prevention pillars EVERY week; power micro-doses MD-2.
competition.intensity: high (low volume preserves quality without fatigue)

programming.source: soccer S&C: off-season rounds out (upper balance) + max-strength base; in-season prehab-heavy (Nordic/Copenhagen van Dyk 2019), congested-fixture aware

playoffs.primaryObjective: Peak freshness + availability for finals/promotion deciders.
playoffs.trainingEmphasis: Minimal-volume high-intensity maintenance; match-day priming; ruthless prioritisation of the pillars.

recovery.primaryObjective: Physical and mental recovery after a 40+ week season; restore tissue; treat carried niggles.
recovery.trainingEmphasis: 2 weeks genuinely off, then unstructured activity, mobility, light cross-training; rehab the season's flags before off-season loading starts.

oneMatchPerWeek.pattern: MD-anchored week: recover, load far from the match, sharpen close to it.
oneMatchPerWeek.heavyDay: MD-4 or MD-3 (lower-body strength + trunk; furthest from both matches)
oneMatchPerWeek.recoveryDay: MD+1 (active recovery + mobility; MD+2 for starters after heavy matches)
oneMatchPerWeek.injuryPreventionDay: primary dose MD-4/MD-3 (Nordic, Copenhagen, calf); never a first Nordic exposure inside MD-2
oneMatchPerWeek.typicalLoadingPattern: MD+1 recovery → MD-4 high (gym heavy) → MD-3 moderate → MD-2 power/speed → MD-1 light priming → MD

twoMatchesPerWeek.pattern: Congested (Sat-Wed-Sat): recovery-first, maintenance micro-doses only between matches — the injury-rate data are unambiguous.
twoMatchesPerWeek.powerDay: optional micro-dose only if >72 h between matches
twoMatchesPerWeek.injuryPreventionDay: low-dose maintenance only (short-lever Copenhagen, low-volume Nordic or isometric substitutes, calf isometrics)
twoMatchesPerWeek.typicalLoadingPattern: Match → recovery → activation/priming → Match → recovery; cut gym volume ~50%; rotate squad where possible.

tournamentOrCongested.pattern: Tournament football (cup weeks, summer tournaments, 3 matches in 8 days) = pure availability management.
tournamentOrCongested.injuryPreventionDay: minimal-dose isometrics (squeeze holds, calf holds, trunk holds)
tournamentOrCongested.typicalLoadingPattern: Protect recovery between fixtures; gym is priming, never development; muscle-injury risk concentrates in the second and third fixtures.

transfersWell: eccentric hamstring work (Nordic) — the single best-evidenced gym intervention in sport
Copenhagen adduction progressions (kicking + cutting groin armour)
single-leg strength (split squat family — every kick and cut is single-leg)
heavy lower-body strength at low volume (squat/trap-bar — correlates with sprint and jump)
low-dose reactive jumps with landing quality (COD stiffness + ACL-protective mechanics)
anti-rotation trunk work (striking force transfer + shielding)
calf/ankle capacity (match running volume + the veteran soleus profile)
limitedValue: bodybuilding-volume upper-body work (mass without match currency)
long steady-state gym cardio (the pitch already supplies conditioning)
sit-up style trunk flexion (adds nothing a braced trunk doesn't do better)
heavy bilateral-only programmes that never load one leg
accessoryPriorities: lateral hip (glute med) work for knee control
gymPhilosophy.singleLegEmphasis: Very high — every strike of the ball is a single-leg stance event and every cut a single-leg push; single-leg strength and control outrank bilateral numbers once a base exists.
gymPhilosophy.olympicLiftingSuitability: Optional — a useful RFD tool if already technical; trap-bar jumps, hip thrusts and sled work deliver most of the benefit at far lower technical cost and are easier to keep in-season.
gymPhilosophy.plyometricEmphasis: Moderate and targeted: the game supplies huge reactive volume, so the gym adds QUALITY — landing mechanics, low-dose stiffness work, aerial-power for CBs/strikers — not quantity.
gymPhilosophy.coreTrainingPhilosophy: The trunk transmits and resists: anti-rotation strength to transfer kicking force from a braced stance leg, lateral-chain strength (side plank/Copenhagen family) for cutting and shielding. No loaded flexion volume.
gymPhilosophy.neckTraining: Low-moderate priority, rising with heading exposure: isometric micro-doses for centre-backs, strikers and set-piece targets; evidence is emerging rather than proven.
gymPhilosophy.gripTraining: Not a priority for outfield players; GK hand/wrist care lives in GK-specific work.
gymPhilosophy.rotationalTraining: Moderate value — anti-rotation first, then low-dose rotational power (cable/med-ball patterns) for strikers and crossers; the kick itself supplies high-velocity rotation daily.
gymPhilosophy.isometricTraining: Valuable in-season: adductor squeeze holds, calf isometrics and trunk holds maintain capacity at minimal soreness cost during congestion.
gymPhilosophy.tempoRecommendations: Controlled eccentrics in robustness phases (hamstring, calf, adductor); explosive intent on all power work.
gymPhilosophy.velocityRecommendations: Heavy-fast intent for strength-speed; light-load maximal-intent jumps and sled work for the acceleration profile; sprinting itself stays on the pitch, programmed and counted.

exercises.name: Nordic hamstring curl
exercises.secondaryAdaptation: sprint-injury protection (~50% risk reduction with adherence)
exercises.sorenessCost: high initially (introduce off-season, never first inside MD-2)

exercises.name: Copenhagen adduction
exercises.secondaryAdaptation: groin-injury protection (41% reduction in the football RCT)

exercises.name: Rear-foot-elevated split squat
exercises.primaryAdaptation: single-leg strength in the plant/strike base
exercises.secondaryAdaptation: hip mobility under load; knee control

exercises.name: Depth jump
exercises.secondaryAdaptation: landing quality under drop load (aerial duels, ACL-relevant mechanics)
exercises.difficulty: advanced (landing quality is the entry ticket)

exercises.name: Calf raise (straight + bent knee)
exercises.secondaryAdaptation: Achilles load tolerance for 10+ km match running

exercises.name: Pallof press
exercises.secondaryAdaptation: kicking force transfer from a braced stance; shielding stability

exercises.name: Lateral band walk
exercises.primaryAdaptation: glute med strength for knee-over-toe control
exercises.secondaryAdaptation: valgus-collapse resistance in cutting and landing

riskFactors: high-speed-running spikes (or ABSENCE — unexposed hamstrings fail on the rare maximal sprint)
warningSigns: reduced sprint confidence / not reaching top speed
injuryPreventionLibrary.recommendedFrequency: Nordic 2x/week building doses (off/pre-season); 1x/week maintenance in-season; PLUS regular counted exposure to >95% max velocity on pitch
exercisesToAvoid: heavy RDL/Nordic novelty the day before matches
monitoringRecommendations: weekly Nordic force or bridge-hold check
high-speed-running exposure counting (GPS or session RPE proxy)
injuryPreventionLibrary.source: Petersen 2011 (RCT, ~60-70% reduction); van der Horst 2015 (amateur RCT); van Dyk 2019 (meta, ~50%); Malone 2017 (sprint exposure)

injuryPreventionLibrary.recommendedFrequency: Copenhagen 2-3x/week (short-lever maintenance in-season) — the Harøy protocol is 3 levels, ~5 min
exercisesToAvoid: sudden maximal kicking volume when flagged
loaded hip adduction novelty in congested weeks
monitoringRecommendations: kicking-volume awareness (count shooting sessions like sprint sessions)

warningSigns: visible valgus on cutting/landing under fatigue
injuryPreventionLibrary.recommendedFrequency: Neuromuscular warm-up (FIFA 11+ pattern) 2-3x/week all season; landing-quality work embedded in gym sessions
exercisesToAvoid: high-volume reactive cutting when fatigued and unprepared
depth jumps without demonstrated landing quality
monitoringRecommendations: hop-test symmetry each block for post-injury players
injuryPreventionLibrary.source: Webster & Hewett 2018 (meta: neuromuscular programmes halve ACL risk); Bizzini & Dvorak 2015; Thorborg 2017 (FIFA 11+)

injuryPreventionLibrary.recommendedFrequency: balance/proprioception 3x/week for 6+ months post-sprain; calf capacity year-round
exercisesToAvoid: reactive cutting volume immediately after a sprain
monitoringRecommendations: single-leg balance checks after any sprain

warningSigns: calf tightness that recurs each match
injuryPreventionLibrary.recommendedFrequency: calf loading 2-3x/week year-round; isometric holds in congested weeks
exercisesToAvoid: sudden surface changes at high volume
monitoringRecommendations: single-leg calf-raise capacity each block (watch it from age 28+)
injuryPreventionLibrary.source: Ekstrand 2011 (calf ~13% of muscle injuries, age-linked); Malliaras 2013 (tendinopathy management)

decisionRules.then: gym is CNS priming only (a few jumps/activation drills) or rest; no strength development
remove high-soreness gym work (Nordic novelty or building doses, heavy eccentrics, new exercises); keep only familiar low-fatigue maintenance
cut gym volume ~50%; maintenance micro-doses only; recovery leads — injury rate is ~6x higher with two matches a week when load is not managed
decisionRules.source: Dupont 2010 (injury rate 25.6 vs 4.1/1000 h with 2 vs 1 matches/week)

decisionRules.then: force a deload week: cap volume, protect availability, flag for review
rebuild gradually — one step down from planned load; no spikes; the pre-season return window is soccer's riskiest

decisionRules.if: readiness score low (poor sleep + soreness + low wellness)
decisionRules.then: autoregulate down one step; quality over volume; do not test
treat as neuromuscular fatigue: reduce CNS-demanding work; recheck in 48 h — especially during fixture congestion
withhold training until symptom-free; resume gradually

hold strength at minimal effective volume (1-2 short heavy sessions/week) — but the Nordic + Copenhagen + calf pillars are NON-NEGOTIABLE weekly items; dropping them in-season is when the injuries they prevent occur
decisionRules.source: Rønnestad & Mujika 2014 (maintenance); van Dyk 2019 + Harøy 2019 (prevention compliance dose-response)

decisionRules.if: high hamstring soreness or Nordic strength drop
decisionRules.then: remove maximal sprint work + heavy eccentric hamstring loading; isometric substitutes; flag — never sprint through a hamstring warning in this sport

decisionRules.if: high adductor/groin soreness or squeeze-test drop >15%
decisionRules.then: cut kicking volume and adductor-loaded gym work to short-lever isometrics; flag — groin problems chronify when trained through
decisionRules.source: Esteve 2015; Harøy 2019 protocol logic; expert consensus

decisionRules.then: reduce intensity one step on arrival days; mobility + easy work

acwr.model: acute (7-day) : chronic (28-day) workload ratio; rolling/EWMA preferred; track high-speed running as its own stream where possible
acwr.source: Gabbett 2016 — methodology contested; used as a conservative guardrail; Malone 2017 for the HSR stream

loadManagement.weeklyProgressionGuideline: Avoid >~10-15% week-to-week spikes, ESPECIALLY in high-speed running and kicking volume; progress ONE stressor at a time (pitch volume, gym load, or sprint/kicking exposure — never all at once). Maintain regular controlled exposure to >95% max velocity — under-exposure is itself a hamstring risk.

gymVolumeRanges.inSeason: low maintenance (1-2 sessions; ~6-10 hard sets/wk per region) + non-negotiable prevention pillars

loadManagement.minimumEffectiveVolume: ~1 heavy low-volume session/week sustains strength in-season; the Nordic + Copenhagen pillars survive even zero-gym weeks (they need a bench and a partner)
loadManagement.maximumAdaptiveVolume: Off-season is the development window — push volume there, not into a 40-week season.
loadManagement.maximumRecoverableVolume: Constrained by match + pitch load and (usually) amateur life load; gym never compromises the next match or the next pitch session.
loadManagement.deloadRecommendations: Planned deload every 3-5 weeks in development phases; automatic deload on ACWR/readiness triggers; congested fixture weeks ARE deload weeks for the gym.
loadManagement.progressionRules: Progress load when reps/quality are met at target RPE and readiness is green.
loadManagement.regressionRules: On red readiness or congested fixtures, drop one step (volume first, intensity second).
loadManagement.missedSessionRules: Never stack missed sessions; resume the planned wave. A missed prevention pillar is rescheduled within the week, not skipped.
loadManagement.source: Gabbett 2016; Dupont 2010; Rønnestad & Mujika 2014; expert consensus

strongEvidence: Nordic hamstring programmes reduce hamstring injury (~50% incidence, more with adherence; L1 — Petersen 2011, van der Horst 2015, van Dyk 2019)
Copenhagen adduction programme reduces groin problems (41%; L1 — Harøy 2019)
FIFA 11+ style neuromuscular warm-ups reduce overall and ACL injury (L1 — Thorborg 2017, Bizzini & Dvorak 2015)
two matches per week multiplies injury rate when load is unmanaged (L2 — Dupont 2010)
maximal squat strength correlates with sprint and jump performance in elite players (L2 — Wisløff 2004)
subjective wellness is a sensitive readiness input (L1 — Saw 2016)
in-season low-volume strength maintenance works (L2 — Rønnestad & Mujika 2014)
weakEvidence: the precise 50% congested-week gym-volume cut (direction certain, magnitude consensus)
position-specific demand splits below professional level
areasRequiringExpertJudgement: balancing pitch vs gym load in congested fixture periods
kicking-volume caps for shooting-heavy roles and dead-ball specialists
managing sprint exposure for low-exposure positions (CB, GK)
female-specific ACL prevention dosing within mixed-resource clubs
areasRequiringFutureResearch: hamstring injury RISE despite Nordic evidence (implementation-compliance gap vs changing match demands — Ekstrand 2016)
artificial turf vs grass injury interaction at amateur level
congestion thresholds for youth and amateur players
potentialRisksIfMisimplemented: introducing Nordic curls at full dose in-season (the soreness injures the week, not the muscle)
heavy posterior-chain work the day before sprint-dense sessions or matches (hamstring risk)
treating the gym as conditioning — the pitch already supplies it; added volume is pure overload
removing all sprint exposure after a hamstring scare (under-exposure raises re-injury risk on return)
chasing squat numbers at the cost of match-week freshness
ignoring the kicking leg / stance leg asymmetry until it presents as injury
